A Cloud-Edge System for Multimodal Clinical Screening in Resource-Constrained Rural Settings A Cloud-Edge System for Multimodal Clinical Screening in Resource-Constrained Rural Settings arXiv:2608.12745v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Medical AI has demonstrated specialist-level diagnostic accuracy, yet these capabilities remain largely inaccessible in resource-constrained rural settings where bandwidth is scarce, compute is limited, and clinical decision-making requires integrating heterogeneous modalities. We introduce a cloud--edge collaborative architecture that addresses these constraints: lightweight, domain-specific models on the edge transform raw medical data into compact structured outputs, while a cloud LLM synthesizes these outputs into clinical summaries. An LLM-based orchestrator dynamically selects diagnostic tools based on patient context, promoting comprehensive modality coverage without processing irrelevant inputs. We evaluate on 20 multimodal clinical cases spanning cardiac, obstetric, trauma, and screening scenarios under three simulated network profiles (500,kbps--5,Mbps). The hybrid system achieves 98--99% diagnostic tool recall with 92--96% precision, matches or exceeds cloud-only baselines on clinical accuracy, and maintains bandwidth-invariant latency (25--35,s) at 4--15x lower token cost. These results highlight the role of architectural design in enabling efficient multimodal integration and improving factual grounding compared to cloud-only approaches under deployment constraints. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: PureTD: Reinforcement Learning for Backgammon Money Games with No Evaluation-time Search
docs.text:
PureTD: Reinforcement Learning for Backgammon Money Games with No Evaluation-time Search PureTD: Reinforcement Learning for Backgammon Money Games with No Evaluation-time Search arXiv:2608.15146v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We revisit Tesauro's TD-Gammon for backgammon money games in the setting of no evaluation-time search. Both checker play and cube action (use of the doubling cube) are learned from scratch via self-play reinforcement learning (RL), with minimal hand-coded logic and no expert features. In this setting, we demonstrate that pure self-play RL suffices to train models that reach near-state-of-the-art playing strength. Specifically, for cubeful money games, our search-free model evaluates faster and is substantially stronger than the open-source engines GNU Backgammon and Open Sage running a one-move (1-ply) look-ahead search. Our method of training a cubeful model also outperforms the standard approach of training a cubeless model and deriving cubeful equity with Janowski-style formulas, when the two models are equally sized. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Conditional Validity for Adaptive Modality Acquisition: When the Policy Chooses Its Own Calibration Group
docs.text:
Conditional Validity for Adaptive Modality Acquisition: When the Policy Chooses Its Own Calibration Group Conditional Validity for Adaptive Modality Acquisition: When the Policy Chooses Its Own Calibration Group arXiv:2608.15520v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: A multimodal system may begin inference while holding only some of its inputs and may acquire the rest at a cost. With adaptive acquisition, the policy determines which inputs are ultimately observed, so we state risk control conditional on that terminal input pattern. Conditional calibration typically assumes that the grouping map is fixed independently of the calibration sample, a condition that policy-induced grouping does not satisfy. We characterize when pattern-conditional risk control remains valid and give two finite-sample constructions: threshold-free routing with calibration applied at the terminal pattern, and simultaneous validation of complete policy-pattern pairs, which lets calibration data select the deployed policy. A counterexample shows that validity proved for a calibration-independent grouping map need not transfer once the policy makes the terminal group calibration-dependent. We call the resulting method RouteCert. On a clinical electrocardiogram task with a staged, cost-ordered lead protocol, the deployed policy answers 71.2% of held-out patients, with an observed 7.4% disagreement with the cardiologist's diagnosis at 48.8% of the prespecified ordinal cost of acquiring each stage, and all three acquisition stages are validated separately. On masked multimodal benchmarks, validating pointwise at each terminal pattern holds observed worst-pattern selective risk, measured against the full-information reference decision rather than the true label, at 0.034, where a pooled design reaches 0.145 against a 0.10 cap, at a comparable answered fraction (0.350 vs 0.342); under the budget-matched simultaneous comparison, the answered fraction falls to 0.305. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Credit Without Ground Truth: Claim-Matched Evaluation of Step-Level Credit with Finite Executed Replay
docs.text:
Credit Without Ground Truth: Claim-Matched Evaluation of Step-Level Credit with Finite Executed Replay Credit Without Ground Truth: Claim-Matched Evaluation of Step-Level Credit with Finite Executed Replay arXiv:2608.19760v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Step-level credit evaluation can conflate numerical association with ordering and branch recovery with position-selection value. We test these distinctions in ALFWorld with two independently seeded replay banks: 27,520 continuations over 172 fixed turns. At 16 continuations per arm per bank, cross-bank replay-contrast associations are Pearson 0.736 and pooled Spearman 0.330. On 30 historical failures, A-count-selected branches at confidence-/implicit-selected positions gain 8.54 percentage points over same-position factual reruns, but their 3.33-point advantage over frozen-random positions under the same alternative-selection rule remains unresolved. Numerical association alone does not establish reliable pooled ordering; branch recovery alone does not establish better score-informed position selection. Historical judge alignment is modestly positive with an unresolved archived-control increment. Same-cohort C/D information-source comparisons and a short, sparse-exposure training pilot provide scope checks; incremental hindsight training utility remains unestablished. Findings are conditional on the tested policies, intervention support and finite budgets. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: HARTS: A Prefix-Sharing Training System for Agentic RL with Hybrid-Attention Models
docs.text:
HARTS: A Prefix-Sharing Training System for Agentic RL with Hybrid-Attention Models HARTS: A Prefix-Sharing Training System for Agentic RL with Hybrid-Attention Models arXiv:2608.28158v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) generates irregular rollout trees, but trajectory-by-trajectory training recomputes their shared interaction histories. Existing training-time prefix-reuse systems do not jointly address state recovery, dense execution, and distributed training for hybrid-attention models. We present HARTS (Hybrid-Attention RL over Tree Structures), to our knowledge the first system to demonstrate training acceleration from arbitrary rollout-tree prefix sharing on real hybrid-attention models. A two-level planner constructs compression-oriented microbatches, then jointly refines their membership, cross-microbatch sharing, placement, and execution order. Within each sharing window, gradients from dependent microbatches accumulate before one backward pass through the shared prefix computation. Differentiable boundary-state handoff and bounded replay preserve the per-trajectory chunkwise numerical path, while a linear-time planner attains the global minimum number of sequential linear-attention calls under our packed chunkwise-call model. The runtime uses a common compact layout across attention and dense or mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers, with support for distributed parallelism and activation recomputation. Recovering log-probabilities for each original trajectory position preserves RL objectives; for deterministic top-k routing without token dropping, occurrence counts restore MoE objective weights and expert-load statistics. On SWE-bench, HARTS delivers 4.77-10.45x the update throughput of trajectory-expanded training across two sampling schemes on 7.9B- and 124B-parameter hybrid-attention MoE models using 8-64 GPUs. On the 7.9B model, full-model logit differences are comparable to baseline self-rerun variation. The 124B model shows stable online learning trends through step 150 on SWE-bench and $\tau^3$-Bench. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: MedCache: Efficient and Temporally Valid Memory for Longitudinal Clinical Agents
docs.text:
MedCache: Efficient and Temporally Valid Memory for Longitudinal Clinical Agents MedCache: Efficient and Temporally Valid Memory for Longitudinal Clinical Agents arXiv:2608.29528v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Longitudinal clinical agents must maintain an evolving patient state from evidence distributed across visits, time points, and specialties. However, how agent memory should be designed for this setting remains unclear. We introduce a benchmark of multi-visit, multi-specialty patient records that evaluates long-context evidence retrieval, cross-time evidence aggregation, and cross-specialty clinical reasoning. Using this benchmark, we systematically study four memory design choices: curation, organization, retrieval, and memory-augmented reasoning. We find that temporal validity is more important than simply retaining more history; specialty-factorized memory reduces context but can hide shared evidence; and multiple agents help when specialists must reason together, not merely when evidence comes from multiple memories. Guided by these findings, we propose \textit{MedCache}, a hybrid framework that constructs temporally valid patient memory, organizes evidence into overlapping specialty views, routes each query to relevant memories, and adaptively invokes one or multiple specialists. Experiments show that MedCache improves reasoning accuracy and memory efficiency over strong single-agent and multi-agent baselines, while generalizing across model backbones and external datasets. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: EEG-VID: Task-Guided Latent Predictive Pretraining for EEG Decoding and Assistive Target Selection
docs.text:
EEG-VID: Task-Guided Latent Predictive Pretraining for EEG Decoding and Assistive Target Selection EEG-VID: Task-Guided Latent Predictive Pretraining for EEG Decoding and Assistive Target Selection arXiv:2609.00566v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We propose EEG-VID, a task-guided latent predictive pretraining framework for EEG decoding under session and subject shifts. EEG-VID predicts future latent EEG states from recent history using an exponential-moving-average target encoder and weak task guidance, followed by supervised fine-tuning. Across VIG-48 and BCI Competition IV-2a/IV-2b, Stage 1 improves mean accuracy in 41 of 42 matched backbone-dataset-protocol comparisons, including all 12 leave-one-subject-out settings, with a maximum gain of 16.22 percentage points. On the 48-region cross-day VIG-48 task, EEG-VID achieves 6.52% Top-1 and 30.50% Top-5 accuracy. In a separate six-participant offline robot-scene study, candidate-constrained target selection reaches 40.24% versus a 25% chance level after subject-specific calibration. These results support task-guided latent prediction as a transferable pretraining strategy for EEG decoding and scene-constrained assistive target selection. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: From Truncation to Commitment: Persistent Context in Uniform Discrete Diffusion
docs.text:
From Truncation to Commitment: Persistent Context in Uniform Discrete Diffusion From Truncation to Commitment: Persistent Context in Uniform Discrete Diffusion arXiv:2609.01043v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Uniform-state discrete diffusion models update all tokens in parallel while keeping every position revisable. Even when the commonly used top-$p$ rule leaves only one candidate at a position, that choice affects only the current reverse step and can be revised at the next sampling step. We ask what changes when selected hypotheses instead become persistent context for later predictions. We therefore propose committed reveal sampling (CRS), a training-free sampler that stores selected argmax tokens and inserts them into subsequent model inputs. Our analysis separates persistent context from truncation. Within one reverse step, adaptive top-$p$, randomized or not, reproduces the update induced by a visible token only when a likelihood-ratio ordering holds, while in a simple latent-mode model, keeping the selected token visible helps later parallel predictions agree on the same sequence-level choice. Empirically, paired experiments on Duo-distilled then separate this persistent effect from single-step top-$p$ restriction and scalar temperature scaling. Under the same finalization rule, CRS without top-$p$ truncation reaches lower generative perplexity (GenPPL) than fixed $p=0.95$ and $p=0.9$ baselines across budgets of 8--64 function evaluations (NFE). At 64 NFE, the comparison at matched unigram entropy also gives lower GenPPL for CRS, shifting the GenPPL--entropy tradeoff under this metric. Base Duo shows the same direction in a descriptive comparison, while other diversity and continuation metrics can rank these operating points differently. A distributional distance to held-out text (SOL) under a fixed GPT-2-Large representation also decreases with persistent context at the same late top-$p$ threshold. These results identify support restriction and persistent context as distinct controls of that tradeoff. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: An Energy-Based Conservative-Dissipative Latent Neural Evolution Operator for Magnetization Dynamics
docs.text:
An Energy-Based Conservative-Dissipative Latent Neural Evolution Operator for Magnetization Dynamics An Energy-Based Conservative-Dissipative Latent Neural Evolution Operator for Magnetization Dynamics arXiv:2609.04530v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We introduce a reduced-order learning framework that couples a convolutional autoencoder to a structured latent neural ordinary differential equation. A learned scalar generates the latent dynamics through an antisymmetric operator and a positive-definite dissipative operator. The antisymmetric component permits motion along scalar level sets, while the dissipative component decreases the scalar. Adding a coercive quadratic term gives bounded continuous-time latent trajectories and approach to the scalar's critical set under the stated assumptions. The scalar provides a structural constraint rather than an approximation of physical energy. The encoder, decoder, scalar, and operators are trained jointly on short snapshot windows without time-derivative supervision, physical-energy labels, or dissipation penalties. At inference, one initial state is encoded and evolved continuously in latent space, with decoding only at requested times. We demonstrate the framework on micromagnetic magnetization trajectories from NIST $\mu$MAG Standard Problem 4 and compare it with dissipative-only dynamics and an unstructured latent neural differential equation. Repeated training runs show competitive observed-horizon accuracy, while selected longer rollouts illustrate improved retention of approximately stationary states relative to the unstructured baseline. These results motivate scalar-generated latent dynamics as an inductive bias for reduced-order prediction and other learning tasks where bounded evolution and equilibrium behavior are important. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Spectral Prioritized Sweeping in Nonstationary Reinforcement Learning
docs.text:
Spectral Prioritized Sweeping in Nonstationary Reinforcement Learning Spectral Prioritized Sweeping in Nonstationary Reinforcement Learning arXiv:2609.06186v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Prioritized Sweeping (PS) accelerates model-based reinforcement learning by selecting backups according to Bellman residual magnitude. In nonstationary reward settings, however, the canonical priority score is shortsighted: after a localized reward shift, residuals propagate only through realized backups, so bottlenecked or topologically distant state estimates may remain static under a limited replanning budget. We introduce the Graph Topology Augmentation framework, which employ the graph's resolvent and its diffusion semantic, to augment the inquired signal. Our application, Graph Topology Augmentation for Prioritized Sweeping (GTA-PS), or which the alias Spectral Prioritized Sweeping (SPS) might be more universal, provides a drop-in ordering score for the setting of fixed dynamics and changing state rewards. GTA-PS uses a smootherized policy, inducing a transition chain, with its in- and out-Laplacian. The standard priority key is augmented with a mixing of regularized Laplacian inverses diffusing the residual magnitude. Furthermore, the topology contribution is annealed by a scheduler based on the Second Largest Eigenvalue Modulus (SLEM), allowing its scale to adapt to the chain's mixing regime. We prove that the forward potential coincides with geometric discounted residual propagation and show that GTA-PS gives active priority instantly to all states. Tabular experiments on FourRooms and GARNET domains demonstrate improved replanning efficiency over standard PS under both exact DP and Dyna-style host planners. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Finite Audits of Model Updating: Coverage and Resolution of Paired Disparity Comparisons
docs.text:
Finite Audits of Model Updating: Coverage and Resolution of Paired Disparity Comparisons Finite Audits of Model Updating: Coverage and Resolution of Paired Disparity Comparisons arXiv:2609.09788v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Finite audits can become more precise and decisive without reliably covering the change in subgroup disparity. We study the updating-minus-frozen difference in absolute subgroup gaps, averaged over a fixed history, for true-positive and false-positive rates separately. Controlled paired-count experiments and independent audits of retained model histories distinguish interval coverage, erroneous conclusions and decision resolution. With a zero frozen gap and a five-percentage-point updating gap, bootstrap coverage is 12.0%; a numerical-delta alternative improves coverage to 52.9%, still far below the nominal 95%, with 500 smaller-group and 2,000 other-group observations of the specified outcome per window over ten windows. Unequal absolute-gap biases explain point-estimate displacement, and gap direction changes pairing's variance contribution. Prior strength materially affects sparse, off-centre comparisons. In the retained panel, relatively high mean coverage coexists with substantial undercoverage for individual histories, while larger audits can considerably improve resolution. Conservative projection provides conditional coverage under the sampling assumptions but often leaves comparisons unresolved. These findings show why interval width and conclusive margin decisions cannot, by themselves, establish the reliability of an estimated disparity change. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Exact Degeneracy Under Balanced k-Shot Sampling:Consequences for Small-Sample Discriminant Analysis on LLM Embeddings
docs.text:
Exact Degeneracy Under Balanced k-Shot Sampling:Consequences for Small-Sample Discriminant Analysis on LLM Embeddings Exact Degeneracy Under Balanced k-Shot Sampling:Consequences for Small-Sample Discriminant Analysis on LLM Embeddings arXiv:2609.09860v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Balanced k-shot sampling, drawing exactly k labeled examples per class, is the standard protocol in few-shot evaluation. We show that it induces an exact degeneracy in Kernelized Linear Principal Component Discriminant Analysis (KLPCDA), a family of seven supervised dimensionality reduction methods. The within-class operator becomes exactly a scaled orthogonal projector, so two variants have all signal eigenvalues equal and a third has a zero operator, and the truncated pseudo-inverse used to implement them removes exactly the subspace that contains all between-class information. We verify this to float64 precision on sentence embeddings and on residual-stream activations of a decoder-only model, and find that the accuracies of the truncated variants change with the number of BLAS threads, by up to 12 percentage points (57 for the variant with a zero operator).
  Replacing the truncation with a ridge selected within the support set, we evaluate few-shot text classification on frozen embeddings (d up to 4096) over four datasets, three embedding models, and three trained baselines. The regularized formulation outperforms the best original variant in 45 of 48 settings, but in general not a tuned linear probe or nearest centroid on bidirectional encoders. Its gains are largest on E5-Mistral, the only decoder-based embedding model, and come from regularized within-class whitening rather than from KLPCDA: shrinkage LDA outperforms both baselines in all 16 E5-Mistral settings, and pre-specified tests show that the effect depends on the embedding model rather than on its dimension. E5-Mistral's remaining gap is largely an estimation-efficiency effect: increasing k to 30-50 reduces the probe's gap to a bidirectional encoder by more than 80%. We give five guidelines limited to the conditions tested and release the code and per-seed results. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: A Machine Learning API for Earth Observation Data Cubes Based on openEO
docs.text:
A Machine Learning API for Earth Observation Data Cubes Based on openEO A Machine Learning API for Earth Observation Data Cubes Based on openEO arXiv:2609.13453v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Earth Observation (EO) data are increasingly organized as spatio-temporal data cubes, while machine learning (ML) methods operate on tabular feature matrices or structured tensor inputs. This mismatch forces platform-specific transformations that are difficult to reproduce or transfer across cloud infrastructures. The openEO specification provides a unified interface for EO data access and processing across heterogeneous backends, but lacks a standardized approach for ML integration.
  We propose a process-level ML specification for openEO structured into three stages: model initialization, model actions (training, tuning, inference, validation), and model management. It supports classical algorithms such as Random Forest and SVM, as well as deep learning architectures for time-series and spatial patch-based modeling, including TempCNN, Temporal Attention Encoders, and foundation model inference. Three prototype implementations in R and Python demonstrate feasibility across diverse technology stacks. A crop type mapping use case demonstrates cross-backend interoperability by submitting an identical process graph to independent R and Python backends and comparing predictions and evaluation metrics.
  Two further use cases demonstrate deep learning on time series and foundation model inference, each executed on a dedicated backend. The prototypes reveal, however, that full cross-backend portability requires deeper harmonization of serialization formats and execution semantics than the process level alone can enforce; backend library versions and preprocessing conventions outside the specification's boundary also affect reproducibility. Addressing both through explicit backend conformance profiles represents the most important near-term direction. The specification advances the reproducibility, portability, and accessibility of ML workflows on EO data cubes across cloud platforms. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Hierarchical GNNs for power flow: letting physics shape the hierarchy
docs.text:
Hierarchical GNNs for power flow: letting physics shape the hierarchy Hierarchical GNNs for power flow: letting physics shape the hierarchy arXiv:2609.26603v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Hierarchical latent communication improves the generalization of a power-flow model, shared across three grids, to new operating scenarios. The module exchanges information through two reduced graphs inside the corrective network of GENCO, replacing two of its local correction steps. We compare Kron-derived transports, a same-anchor Quotient construction and the flat GENCO Base architecture, all trained under one protocol of our own with about a hundred times fewer optimizer updates per grid than GENCO's reference training: 200 epochs on three grid topologies, fewer than 1,900 training scenarios per grid and three initialization seeds per model. Evaluation uses 200 newly generated, preselected scenarios per grid. On the training topologies, Kron reaches a macro family-balanced voltage error of $0.851\pm0.110$, 51.3% below a per-bus mean fitted on training solutions (1.747). Kron is below this reference on 98.5% of the 600 fresh scenarios, and both hierarchical models outperform it on every training topology in all three seeds. The flat baseline reaches $5.660\pm0.899$ and does not outperform the reference on any training topology, so Kron's 85.0% reduction relative to it compares architectures within our training regime. Kron is also 31.0% below Quotient ($1.235\pm0.225$). These results demonstrate generalization across operating scenarios within the studied topologies, with one set of learned parameters shared across grids. On two topologies unseen in training, the current models do not yet outperform the fitted reference in calibrated transfer; extrapolation to new topologies is the next development objective. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Bayesian Optimization with Fisher Information Geometry: Gradient Bounds and Trust-Region Methods
docs.text:
Bayesian Optimization with Fisher Information Geometry: Gradient Bounds and Trust-Region Methods Bayesian Optimization with Fisher Information Geometry: Gradient Bounds and Trust-Region Methods arXiv:2609.31107v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We study Bayesian optimization (BO) through the lens of information geometry. Pulling back the Fisher information metric through the surrogate posterior map yields a local sensitivity tensor on the input space, which leads to an upper bound on the gradient of reparameterizable acquisition functions. This view explains vanishing-gradient behavior in high-dimensional BO and provides a common interpretation of heuristics such as RAASP and dimension-scaled lengthscales. Building on this analysis, we propose FITR, a trust-region-based BO method that replaces lengthscale-based scaling by local pullback-Fisher weights. FITR is not restricted to GP kernels with explicit lengthscales. On GP benchmarks with an SE kernel, experiments show competitive performance using FITR. The proposed method also easily generalizes to non-isotropic surrogates, although the gains are more task-dependent in that setting. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: DisCoMBO: Steering Expert-in-the-Loop Black-Box Optimization via Distributional Conformance
docs.text:
DisCoMBO: Steering Expert-in-the-Loop Black-Box Optimization via Distributional Conformance DisCoMBO: Steering Expert-in-the-Loop Black-Box Optimization via Distributional Conformance arXiv:2609.36472v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Sequential Model-Based Optimization (SMBO) traditionally relies on Bayesian or ensembling surrogates for uncertainty quantification. While historically treated as fully data-driven, SMBO increasingly integrates external domain expertise to accelerate discovery. To overcome the opaque guidance and diminished integration fidelity of standard acquisition re-weighting, Probabilistic Circuits (PCs) have emerged as a generative surrogate alternative, enabling direct knowledge injection via conditional sampling. However, these generative routines lack the formal exploration-exploitation semantics required for rigorous optimization. We introduce the Distributional Conformance Score (DisCo), a novel metric that unifies the flexibility and efficiency of PCs with a formal uncertainty framework. DisCo provides a bounded, $[0, 1]$-normalized measure of model "surprise" that (1) recovers properties comparable to kernel-based uncertainty known from, e.g., Gaussian Processes, while maintaining linear-time inference, and (2) enables accurate assessment of conformance of external knowledge w.r.t. model evidence. We then present DisCoMBO, a framework leveraging these properties for robust, knowledge-aware optimization. We prove that DisCoMBO is a zero-regret algorithm and demonstrate its effectiveness across diverse benchmarks from AutoML, material optimization, and wind park optimization. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: LongSpark: Efficient speculative decoding with a fixed-cost parallel drafter
docs.text:
LongSpark: Efficient speculative decoding with a fixed-cost parallel drafter LongSpark: Efficient speculative decoding with a fixed-cost parallel drafter arXiv:2609.37029v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive inference by verifying multiple draft tokens in a single target forward pass. However, as the context grows, existing state-of-the-art drafters become increasingly expensive, eroding the very efficiency advantage they are designed to provide. We argue that this scaling is unnecessary. A standalone language model must grow with its prefix because it is solely responsible for every token it produces. A drafter, by contrast, only proposes candidates; the target catches and corrects every error before any token is committed. The drafter's decoding cost can therefore be made entirely independent of the prefix length. We introduce LongSpark, a block-diffusion drafter that achieves this by extracting fixed-size, multiscale views from the target's verification pass, thereby eliminating the need for a growing persistent state. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that LongSpark achieves state-of-the-art end-to-end efficiency across multiple model scales and realistic serving conditions. Notably, it delivers the lowest time-per-output-token on long-context tasks while reducing the drafter's context state by several orders of magnitude. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Non-Commutative Lie-Algebraic State-Space Models: Finite-Division Variety Laws, Semidirect Cascades, and Gradient Saddle Escape
docs.text:
Non-Commutative Lie-Algebraic State-Space Models: Finite-Division Variety Laws, Semidirect Cascades, and Gradient Saddle Escape Non-Commutative Lie-Algebraic State-Space Models: Finite-Division Variety Laws, Semidirect Cascades, and Gradient Saddle Escape arXiv:2610.00329v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Structured state-space models (SSMs) achieve linear-time inference and logarithmic-time parallel training via associative scans, yet homogeneous diagonal transitions generate solvable semigroups unable to track non-solvable group words or 3D rigid-body manifolds. We develop a theoretical and empirical framework for Non-Commutative Lie-Algebraic State-Space Models (Lie-SSMs), parameterizing recurrent updates on Lie algebra tangent spaces via the matrix exponential. First, via an o-minimal multi-rate cylindrical flag collar, we establish an unconditional single-layer finite-division criterion for homogeneous contracting $SO(3)$ and $SU(2)$ heads, proving odd-prime Sylow abelianity, odd-$p$-core centrality $[u^2,x]=e$, exponent-30 commutator laws ($[u^{30},v^{30}]=e$ in $SO(3)^m$ and $[u^{30},v^{30}]\in Z(G),[u^{30},v^{30}]^2=e$ in $SU(2)^m,SO(4)^m$, excluding $S_5$), and sharp threshold $d^*(S_5)=d^*(A_6)=5$ in $SO(5)$. Second, Depth-2 semidirect and Schreier $2$-cocycle cascades resolve $S_5$, $2I\cong SL_2(F_5)$, and $\mathrm{Heis}(F_p)$ in $O(\log T)$ depth, whereas unnormalized contracting coupling collapses exponentially without Directional RMSNorm. Third, we characterize the $O(\varepsilon^{c-1})$ Chen--Magnus--Hall--Witt commutator saddle and $1/|[G,G]|$ coset-centroid dilution, proving $\varepsilon=0$ symmetry breaking and local Polyak--\L{}ojasiewicz convergence ($\theta_{\max}<\pi$), solving $S_5$ ($99.90\%/99.40\%$ at $T=128$) and $D_{16}$ ($100.00\%$) via dense prefix loss and factored readouts. Across $Q_8,A_5,S_5,D_{16}$, Dyck-2, $SE_2(3)$ Left-Jacobian odometry, GPU scans ($26.03\times$ speedup), and three 3D IMU cohorts (UCI HAR, HAPT-PT 30-subject CV, and REALDISP), Depth-2 Lie-$SO(3)$ cascades reach $95.69\%\pm 0.14\%$ on HAR, $87.16\%\pm 0.64\%$ ($88.32\%\pm 0.93\%$ 30-subject episodes) on HAPT-PT, and $84.23\%\pm 1.00\%$ under displacement on REALDISP. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Geometry-Dependent Online and Offline Approximation for Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization
docs.text:
Geometry-Dependent Online and Offline Approximation for Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization Geometry-Dependent Online and Offline Approximation for Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization arXiv:2610.00545v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We study online and offline maximization of nonnegative, non-monotone DR-submodular functions over compact convex down-closed sets $K\subseteq[0,1]^d$ that contain a supplied diagonal point $\zeta\mathbf{1}$. Our online algorithm earns at least $\underline{\alpha}(\zeta)=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{(1-2\zeta)_+^2}{2(3-2\zeta)^2}$ times the reward of the best fixed feasible point, minus $O(\sqrt{T})$, using one possibly stochastic gradient query and one projection per round; $\underline{\alpha}(0)=4/9$. One post-decision noisy value query per round gives $O(T^{3/4})$ regret, and two exact value queries give $O(\sqrt{T})$. Conversely, no offline algorithm with polynomially many exact value-and-gradient queries attains a coefficient above an explicit $\beta_*\approx 0.4704$ at $\zeta=0$, improving the bound $2(e^{-1/2}-e^{-1})\approx 0.478$ of Oveis Gharan and Vondr\'ak (2011); for $\zeta>0$, two families of hard instances give an upper bound that we reduce exactly to finitely many convex problems below $\zeta=1/8$ and give in closed form above it. The bound $\beta_*$ also holds for nonnegative submodular set functions under a cardinality constraint, improving the previous $0.478$. Online-to-offline conversion gives $\underline{\alpha}(\zeta)-\varepsilon$ offline, and the upper bound also limits online learners with polynomial query budgets and uniform $O(T^\kappa)$ regret, $\kappa<1$. Both coefficients equal $1/2$ for $\zeta\ge 1/2$ and fall short of $1/2$ by order $(1/2-\zeta)^2$ below. For quadratic objectives we attain $1/2$, and for cubic objectives $\max\{8/17,\,2\sqrt{3-4r}/(1+\sqrt{3-4r})^2\}$ with $r=\min\{\zeta,1/2\}$. For submodular set functions, rounding the multilinear extension gives $\underline{\alpha}(\zeta)-\varepsilon$ under a matroid whose polytope contains $\zeta\mathbf{1}$ and $4/9-\varepsilon$ under a fixed number of knapsack constraints. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: PIT-GCL: Protein Interaction using Topological Graph Contrastive Learning
docs.text:
PIT-GCL: Protein Interaction using Topological Graph Contrastive Learning PIT-GCL: Protein Interaction using Topological Graph Contrastive Learning arXiv:2610.04850v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Protein binding prediction is central to target identification, therapeutic binder design, and large scale screening, yet remains challenging because binding depends on sequence, three dimensional geometry, and global structural organization. Recent folding models such as AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2 have substantially improved structure prediction, but their confidence outputs (pLDDT, pTM, ipTM) are not specifically designed for binary binding prediction, and dedicated structure aware predictors often require bound complex structures that are unavailable at screening scale. We introduce PIT-GCL, a dual tower structure aware framework that encodes each protein independently from its amino acid sequence, C{\alpha} point cloud, and a global persistent homology descriptor. Each tower combines residue ESM-2 embeddings with a topological summary computed from the H0 and H1 persistence landscapes of a Vietoris-Rips filtration, and processes the resulting tokens with a structure aware Transformer in which pairwise C{\alpha} distances enter as a learned attention bias. A bidirectional cross attention module then performs latent space soft docking between the two per-protein representations, and the model is trained with a combined binary cross entropy and NT-Xent contrastive objective. On three binary interaction prediction benchmarks, general PPI on PPIRef, TCRpMHC binding on STAG, and whole chain pairs on PPB-Affinity, PIT-GCL outperforms representative sequence based, structure aware, and task specific baselines on general PPI under our evaluation, and is the only method above chance on PPB-Affinity; on TCR-pMHC it leads at a fixed decision threshold but is outranked by a task specific sequence model. Because each protein is encoded independently in the first phase, its representation can be precomputed and reused across candidate pairs, which is convenient for large scale screening. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Greedy Local Learning for Language Model Pretraining: Gaps and Objective Design
docs.text:
Greedy Local Learning for Language Model Pretraining: Gaps and Objective Design Greedy Local Learning for Language Model Pretraining: Gaps and Objective Design arXiv:2610.04867v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Greedy block-wise local learning splits a network into gradient-isolated blocks trained by local auxiliary losses, deleting the backward pass between blocks: inter-stage communication becomes forward-only and every block can step its optimizer independently, properties directly relevant to decentralized model-parallel training. Local learning is competitive with end-to-end backpropagation on image classification, and on small Transformers it is known to trade a worse best loss for parallel speedup. How this loss gap behaves in autoregressive language model (LM) pretraining at larger scale, and which auxiliary designs reduce it, has not been measured. We present a token-budget-matched empirical study at 125M and 400M parameters with $K \in \{1,2,4\}$ blocks at Chinchilla-optimal budgets, factorizing the auxiliary design into network architecture and training objective. We observe: (i) the gap to end-to-end training more than doubles from $K=2$ to $K=4$, but at $K=4$ shrinks from 125M to 400M; (ii) replacing an MLP auxiliary with a Transformer-based one is a strong network-side intervention, recovering 22-41% of the gap; (iii) a multi-token-prediction (MTP) auxiliary objective helps at the first block boundary, whereas adding it at deeper boundaries hurts, and restricting it to the first block yields the best $K=4$ configuration ($+0.062$ vs. $+0.075$ nats at 400M); and (iv) deployment-style per-block execution reduces activation memory by up to $2.2\times$. We frame these results as an empirically grounded method direction rather than a finalized method: local objectives should apply future-predictive pressure selectively across boundaries while resisting shortcuts that bypass predictive content. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: What Does a Harness Repair? A Preregistered Study of Visibility, Baseline Adequacy and Evaluation Defects
docs.text:
What Does a Harness Repair? A Preregistered Study of Visibility, Baseline Adequacy and Evaluation Defects What Does a Harness Repair? A Preregistered Study of Visibility, Baseline Adequacy and Evaluation Defects arXiv:2610.05533v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Harness search keeps a change to the prompts, token budgets or parsers around a frozen model if the change raises a score. Such a gain can come from answers the parser could not read before, a weak comparison or an evaluation defect. We preregistered two studies of where these gains come from, with three models of 1.7B to 8B parameters and with Qwen3-14B, and report all 65 primary endpoints. Turning thinking off raised accuracy over a capped thinking setting in 7 of 12 model-benchmark cells, each time mostly through questions the capped setting left without a readable answer. For the small models, the thinking-off setting was not meaningfully worse than a rescue configuration in 7 of 9 cells, nor, for the 1.7B model, than four GEPA-selected harnesses. At 14B, two GEPA harnesses beat it by 30 to 34 points on the LongevityBench letter tasks; in descriptive analyses they were not detectably above the strongest constant-label baseline and answered "Yes" in 95% to 99% of their parsed mortality answers. From a start capped at 64 tokens, GEPA repaired the 1.7B model's harness, but at 14B no proposal of either search scored above zero. Replication through the same pipeline reproduced a defect's distortion in 9 of 20 evaluable cases, 7 of them cases in which the distortion is fixed by an identity of the design. Descriptively, relative to its base model, longevity fine-tuning raised a 1.7B model's letter accuracy by 41 points and cut its MMLU-Pro and GSM8K accuracy by 16 and 63 points; on a second GPU, 58% of its zero-temperature token sequences changed and none of the nine grid verdicts we rechecked did. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Where Do LLMs Retrieve Network Information? Identifying the Responsible Heads and Neurons
docs.text:
Where Do LLMs Retrieve Network Information? Identifying the Responsible Heads and Neurons Where Do LLMs Retrieve Network Information? Identifying the Responsible Heads and Neurons arXiv:2610.08200v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) used for Web information processing rely on retrieving relationships between network entities, such as domain names and IP addresses, but the internal components that causally enable this retrieval remain unclear, hindering targeted safeguards against unsafe actions. Therefore, we investigate whether their retrieval capabilities can be localized to specific attention heads or individual neurons within these LLMs. Across five LLMs from three architecture families, we identify heads through causal ablation screening, test their selectivity against matched negative and context-free controls, rank neurons within these heads using causal ablation and correlational measures, and leverage features from both causally validated heads and individual neurons to build network information retrieval detectors, which we evaluate without retraining on an independent reverse-DNS dataset. In every model, a small set of causally validated heads (1--9 out of 128--1152 candidates) builds a detector with 99.5--100\% held-out accuracy. At the neuron level, the results are model-specific, e.g., in one model, causal and correlational rankings identify the same neuron, matching full-head performance (AUC = 1.000), while in another, the best causally ranked neuron achieves only AUC = 0.665 despite the full head reaching 1.000. On independent CAIDA data, head detectors maintain AUC $\geq 0.971$, while single-neuron detectors fall below chance in three of five models. Overall, these findings highlight the importance of choosing an appropriate level of granularity when causally localizing how LLMs retrieve structured network information from context. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Pick the Mixture, Not the Samples: Combinatorial Data Selection for LLMs
docs.text:
Pick the Mixture, Not the Samples: Combinatorial Data Selection for LLMs Pick the Mixture, Not the Samples: Combinatorial Data Selection for LLMs arXiv:2610.14028v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Data selection for LLM fine-tuning faces two facts about real training: data pools draw from many distinct domains, and evaluation spans diverse tasks. As a result, the same sample helps different tasks differently, and samples interact during training so that a subset's value is not the sum of its parts. Current data-selection methods leave these realities largely unaddressed. We formalize them as Combinatorial Data Selection (CDS), a framework that separates attribution (how samples are scored) from selection (which subset to pick) and models the non-additive interactions among samples. On a real instruction-tuning data pool, we find substantial cross-domain complementarity (joint utility exceeds the sum of singletons), alongside redundancy within domains. Inspired by this, we propose Mixture-then-Select, a two-stage algorithm that first decides how many samples to take from each domain, then ranks samples within each domain by attribution score. Theoretically, the gap to the optimal subset is linear in the selection size and independent of data pool size. Empirically, Mixture-then-Select outperforms strong baselines by 20 to 54%, is robust across attribution methods, and works across different models and data pool sizes. The framework also extends to the data purchasing problem under a budget constraint when sample prices vary. Our findings suggest that allocating selection across domains offers a promising path toward more efficient and effective data selection for modern LLMs. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Matched Specialization, Different Adaptation: Second-Moment Structure in Shared Representations
docs.text:
Matched Specialization, Different Adaptation: Second-Moment Structure in Shared Representations Matched Specialization, Different Adaptation: Second-Moment Structure in Shared Representations arXiv:2610.15830v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Small Adam-trained shared-representation networks can reach equivalent selected mean readout measurements yet respond differently to the same further learning. We use state interventions to separate second-moment scale and coordinate-pattern effects, then examine their formation and time dependence. In the central two-target experiment, the more precisely readable target switches within ten updates in 67.5% of acquisition-formed checkpoints and 0% of update-formed checkpoints. First-moment exchange leaves the ten-update contrast change within its pre-specified margin, whereas second-moment exchange reverses the contrast. A coordinate-pattern effect remains at common mean adaptive scale. Layer and movement controls locate an effect beyond overall update size. Formation records connect small encoder second moments with stronger cancellation between task gradients. A prospective gradient-projection experiment changes this retained state; transferring the resulting second moment alone reduces the ten-update adaptation response in a fixed recipient. The matched comparison extends to three Gaussian targets, while a room-sensor extension retains component effects but fails endpoint matching. Across tested regimes, component effects survive more widely than reversal or reset equivalence. Effect magnitude and duration depend on learning conditions. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Resample the Answer: Where to Spend Test-Time Compute in Recursive Reasoning
docs.text:
Resample the Answer: Where to Spend Test-Time Compute in Recursive Reasoning Resample the Answer: Where to Spend Test-Time Compute in Recursive Reasoning arXiv:2610.16427v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recursive reasoning models such as the Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) iteratively refine two latent states: an answer state y, decoded into the output, and a reasoning state z, which is never decoded. Many of their failures have been attributed to bad basins, regions of latent space that trap the recursion on wrong answers. Recent test-time approaches perturb y, z or both to recover these failures, but the impact of this choice on performance, test-time compute efficiency and scaling properties remains unclear. Through controlled experiments on TRM, we find that a failed trajectory carries its failure in its answer state. At equal compute, whether retries continue a failed trajectory (depth scaling) or draw multiple trajectories from the initial states (width scaling), resampling y recovers more failures than any perturbation of z we tested, and the performance gap widens as the test-time compute budget grows. Our approach, Gated Answer Resampling (GAR), pairs this resampling of the answer state with the model's own halting head and restarts only the puzzles that the head rejects. With at most 64 restarts per puzzle and no training or hyperparameter search, GAR takes TRM from 85.9% to 99.4% on Sudoku-Extreme and from 68.8% to 85.6% on Pencil Puzzle Bench validation. On the same checkpoints, GAR also outperforms Probabilistic TRM (PTRM), which perturbs z at each step, even when PTRM uses 42 to 197 times as much compute. Our code is available at https://github.com/MaximeILL/GAR. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Comparing GenAI to Machine Learning and Manual Review for eDiscovery
docs.text:
Comparing GenAI to Machine Learning and Manual Review for eDiscovery Comparing GenAI to Machine Learning and Manual Review for eDiscovery arXiv:2610.16925v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Keeling et al. [Keeling2026Generative] report on a case study recently conducted by Redgrave LLP in which they assert that Relativity's Generative AI Review tool (aiR) achieved 88% recall while Relativity Assisted Learning (RAL), its machine-learning tool, achieved 64% recall. These results are not comparable because the methods employed have different objectives, because of inter-assessor disagreement, and because they represent different recall-precision and cost-benefit trade-offs. Our analysis of the Redgrave data indicates that, when these differences are taken into account, aiR and manual review are comparable. Furthermore, established machine-learning models employing Continuous Active Learning (CAL) and Scalable Continuous Active Learning (S-CAL) show state-of-the-art effectiveness, and superior efficiency, when trained only on a sample of 2,000 first-pass-reviewer responsiveness determinations. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: MAGNET: Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network for Connectome Generation
docs.text:
MAGNET: Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network for Connectome Generation MAGNET: Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network for Connectome Generation arXiv:2610.17014v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Functional brain connectome represents neural connectivity as a matrix of pairwise interactions between brain regions. Generation of functional connectomes is not only a question of validity; rather, having satisfied the constraints on the correlation matrix, the next step is to recover the class-conditional geometry buried under coarse labels. We propose MAGNET, a Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network which uses a normalized-Cholesky representation of the manifold of correlation matrices that guarantees validity. MAGNET lifts noisy latent states into ROI-level region tokens and performs denoising with a relational inductive bias over brain atlas regions. To deal with structural problems induced by coarse labels, MAGNET employs class-anchored conditioning, amortized structural bridge, and relevance-preserving corruption. Across ABIDE, ADNI, and OASIS-3, MAGNET consistently achieves favorable results compared to previous manifold-aware approaches, demonstrating improvements of 7-21% in class-conditional fidelity ($\alpha,\beta$-F1) across three cohorts and better sampling efficiency. Moreover, while training only with strict binary labels, MAGNET is capable of maintaining clinical heterogeneity through fine substructure of the connectomes in a zero-shot setting, improving subclass covariance alignment ($\lambda$-MSE) by over 30%. These results suggest that geometric validity is a necessary but insufficient condition for clinical utility in connectome synthesis. Moreover, efforts in making the diffusion denoising class-conditional manifold aware finds utility beyond the highly curved brain connectome generation as this is a critical problem in various general settings. The code repository can be found at https://github.com/protyayofficial/MAGNET. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning
docs.text:
ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning arXiv:2610.18683v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) agents, yet efficient critic-free algorithms (e.g., GRPO) suffer from a fundamental uniform credit assignment dilemma that broadcasts trajectory-level advantages equally to all actions. Our analysis reveals that this uniformity inherently reinforces structurally unreasonable actions in preferred trajectories and ignores each action's downstream deviations in unpreferred ones. To resolve this without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a plug-and-play framework that leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive experiments across Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct demonstrate that ProAS universally elevates mainstream group-based baselines to new state-of-the-art performance, achieving peak success rates of 91.9% and 94.3% on ALFWorld, alongside 66.7% and 70.8% on WebShop, respectively. Furthermore, it accelerates training convergence by up to $2.44\times$ while maintaining strong robustness against imperfect or distilled ARGs. Codes: https://github.com/LINs-lab/ProAS アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Refined Topology-Pass Scheduling: Damped Trust-Region Compensation for Dynamic k-NN Graphs in SE(3)-Equivariant Structure Prediction
docs.text:
Refined Topology-Pass Scheduling: Damped Trust-Region Compensation for Dynamic k-NN Graphs in SE(3)-Equivariant Structure Prediction Refined Topology-Pass Scheduling: Damped Trust-Region Compensation for Dynamic k-NN Graphs in SE(3)-Equivariant Structure Prediction arXiv:2610.19246v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Equivariant structure-prediction pipelines alternate coordinate updates with the construction of a k-nearest-neighbour (kNN) graph whose membership is a discrete, piecewise-constant function of the coordinates. Rebuilding that graph at every block boundary (PB) is the expensive part of an epoch, whereas reusing one frozen graph (F) is fast but leaves a topology gap. We study a two-pass design in which the cheap pass records a small amount of state (margins, kNN radii, measured per-boundary displacements) and a second pass compensates conservatively. We formulate the choice of the graph-construction basis as a damped fixed-point iteration whose unique fixed point is exactly PB, and derive (i) exact non-flip certificates with the two-sided constant $m_i/4$ and one-sided constant $m_i/2$, (ii) the minimum-variance (BLUE) replay gain $\gamma^*$ and the resulting feasibility crossover, (iii) an $\ell_\infty$ trust-region projection that preserves convergence, and (iv) an analytic near-tie spacing law $E[m] \approx r_k/(3k)$ that matches measurements to 1\%. Three compensation levels are implemented in C++ (L1: frozen set with live geometry; L2: margin-gated local repair; L3: damped, projected basis) and validated under a matched-conditions protocol (identical seed, MSA depth and trajectory family, only the topology mode differs). L2 reproduces the PB edge set exactly ($D = 0.0000$ at every boundary), L1 stays within 0.6% and L3 interpolates monotonically: L2 reproduces the PB edge set exactly when the trust region is removed, and L3 interpolates between the frozen and the PB topology. The recorded trajectory itself yields a measured $1.5\times$ Pass-1 and $1.76\times$ epoch speed-up with no measurable loss gap. An open-source implementation of the runtime and of all the experiments reported here is available at https://github.com/AlbertHuang96/ProteinPredictMachineLearning. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Continuum Attention
docs.text:
Continuum Attention Continuum Attention arXiv:2610.20586v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Conventional causal attention aggregates values at discrete memory positions. We introduce Continuum Attention (CA), in which neighboring key and value vectors define a continuous, piecewise linear memory trajectory and each query retrieves information by normalized integration over its visible prefix. The segment integrals have closed forms in exponential moments, yielding analytically differentiable attention without numerical quadrature. The resulting operator preserves causal masking, normalized nonnegative effective weights, and the standard Transformer decoder structure. Controlled byte level experiments favor exact continuous integration over matched softmax attention. We additionally evaluate data efficiency, out of domain language modeling, zero-shot multiple choice prediction, robustness, and multilingual generalization. In multilingual evaluation, CA consistently outperforms all baselines across every evaluated language, achieving an average 5.8% reduction in bits per byte (BPB) relative to the strongest baseline. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: StochLOB: Heavy-Tailed Score Matching for Robust Limit Order Book Trend Prediction
docs.text:
StochLOB: Heavy-Tailed Score Matching for Robust Limit Order Book Trend Prediction StochLOB: Heavy-Tailed Score Matching for Robust Limit Order Book Trend Prediction arXiv:2610.21081v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Score-based diffusion methods usually perturb data with Brownian Gaussian noise, corresponding to a light-tailed forward stochastic differential equation (SDE). For market time series this SDE can be a poor abstraction: limit order book (LOB) order flow is heavy-tailed, bursty, and occasionally jump-like. We study STOCHLOB, a training-only score-matching framework that changes the forward diffusion corruption law while leaving the deployed predictor deterministic. Instead of Brownian-only Gaussian corruption, the noising process uses two non-Gaussian SDE-inspired alternatives: jump-L\'evy noise through a compound-Poisson variance mixture, and clipped $\alpha$-stable noise through a positive-stable Gaussian scale mixture. These corruptions inject finite jumps and heavy-tailed residuals into training without requiring reverse-time diffusion sampling at inference. The resulting score target has a useful interpretation: its radial factor $h_t(r)$ is the posterior expected corruption precision, so large residuals are weighted according to the latent corruption scale that most plausibly generated them. On chronologically held-out Coinbase LOB data, the proposed variants remain competitive on uncorrupted BTC and altcoin test horizons and improve several realized tail-window stress diagnostics. An exploratory Feishu A-share transfer study further tests whether the probability outputs remain usable under transaction costs and trading-rule constraints. Code and configuration files are available at https://github.com/ArshiAbolghasemi/Penny. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction
docs.text:
On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction arXiv:2610.22543v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) promise parallel text generation, but in practice face an unresolved speed-quality trade-off. Exact decoding fills in only one masked position per model pass, while faster multi-token decoding schemes are lossy. Speculative decoding is the standard lossless acceleration for autoregressive models. However, it does not transfer directly to DLMs, which must choose both what to generate and where. We show that this order is the missing piece: the model's own predictions from the previous pass already give the right token at over $90\%$ of positions, but not which position comes next. We introduce Speculating Positions Order Trajectory (SPOT), a 0.62M-parameter model that reads only the target's output distributions, predicts this order and proposes a tree of candidate continuations, which the target verifies in a single pass by state equality. Coupled-noise match, which shares Gumbel noise between drafter and target, keeps this verification exact at any temperature. This approach also inspired us to introduce SPOT-Sets for dynamic threshold decoding, where a pass commits several positions: SPOT-Sets drafts whole commit sets together with their tokens. Our comprehensive experiments show that SPOT cuts target passes by up to $6.8\times$ and reaches up to $3.4\times$ the throughput of standard decoding on SDAR-8B, matching or beating the calibrated and training-free drafting baselines in every task and budget at $T=0$ and $T=1$. In addition, we show that SPOT's learned drafter transfers across models, demonstrating successful transfer across six different DLMs; with a light calibration, the SPOT-Sets drafter transfers as well. On top of dynamic threshold decoding, SPOT-Sets improves the throughput of SDAR-8B by 59% on average over the threshold decoder alone. Project page: https://eliezer318.github.io/SPOT-dLLM/ アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Choosing models for network-wide freeway speed estimation and forecasting from sparse fixed sensors
docs.text:
Choosing models for network-wide freeway speed estimation and forecasting from sparse fixed sensors Choosing models for network-wide freeway speed estimation and forecasting from sparse fixed sensors arXiv:2610.22630v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Most freeway agencies have fixed detectors on only part of their network but need speeds for all of it. This paper compares methods for estimating current and next-hour speeds on every link from such sparse detectors, using historical probe data for training. The test network is the Dallas--Fort Worth freeway system: 4,127 directional links, of which 643 (15.6\%) carry a side-fire detector. Eighteen methods from five families (non-learned baselines, statistical estimators, tabular learners, road-graph neural networks and models that learn spatial relations) were trained under one protocol with three random seeds. Each neural architecture was also retrained with a parameter-free, direction-aware kernel interpolation of the sensor readings as additional input. Graph neural networks that pass information along the road graph, including a plain graph convolutional recurrent network, reduced the current-hour error on unsensored links by about 17\% relative to the historical average. Models with adaptive graphs, attention or identity embeddings stayed close to the historical average and did not fit the training data well, indicating that they could not learn which detectors matter for which links. With the interpolation features, all ten architectures came within about 0.1 mph of each other. The remaining error depended mainly on coverage: almost all of the improvement was found within about 3 mi of a detector, and very little on tollways without detectors or on links with no road-graph connection to one. The results are summarised as guidance on model choice and detector placement. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Announced Breaks Separate Conformal Reliability from Frequency Calibration
docs.text:
Announced Breaks Separate Conformal Reliability from Frequency Calibration Announced Breaks Separate Conformal Reliability from Frequency Calibration arXiv:2610.23917v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Many structural breaks are announced in advance, yet adaptive conformal methods learn of them only from their own errors. A reset at the announced date serves one of two audits, conformal reliability of the next interval or frequency calibration of a closed window, and the two can disagree. For independent scores, restarting the empirical quantile at the boundary attains the minimax reliability rate, of order one over the square root of the post-break count. Restarting an adaptive recursion attains a frequency gap of order one over that count on bounded scores when its floor adds a bounded total. That gap bounds nothing about the next interval. After a large synthetic break, the restarted quantile's coverage error at the 50th forecast is 0.035, against 0.052 for the best of five adaptive baselines. The restarted recursion has the smallest frequency gap over the first 50 forecasts after every synthetic break. Real breaks are mostly smaller. The restarted quantile beats two baselines after an electricity market reform and trails all five after monetary policy decisions. Of nine announced breaks screened, only one is large enough for a detectable gain, and there every method misses nominal coverage by more than 0.1. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: A learner-free swarm reaches the explore-exploit equilibrium: A self-organized attractor approximating the reinforcement-learning solution
docs.text:
A learner-free swarm reaches the explore-exploit equilibrium: A self-organized attractor approximating the reinforcement-learning solution A learner-free swarm reaches the explore-exploit equilibrium: A self-organized attractor approximating the reinforcement-learning solution arXiv:2610.25113v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The explore-exploit trade-off is the core problem of reinforcement learning (RL). In its multi-agent, resource-sharing form the optimum is not a scalar-return maximum but an equilibrium allocation -- the ideal-free distribution (IFD), the Nash equilibrium of a congestion game. We show that a minimal foraging swarm reaches the shape of this equilibrium as a self-organized attractor -- foragers in proportion to resource richness (matching slope 0.94) -- with no learner, no trained parameters, and no payoff or reward read anywhere in its dynamics. Agents explore by heavy-tailed (Levy) flights, recruit neighbours to a discovery through a threshold cascade on their proximity network, and disperse as a patch crowds; removing the coupling of recruitment to movement collapses the matching (slope 0.08). The reinforcement learning is at the level of the problem and the allocation reached, not the micro-rule. The swarm reaches this equilibrium rather than learning it, attaining its shape but not the exact equilibrium: it stays measurably exploitable (Nash-gap 0.58 versus ~0.01 for a converged learner). Against PPO learners (feedforward, centralized-critic, and graph message-passing) trained in the same sensing-limited environment, the reward-free swarm at zero training matches the IFD gradient more faithfully than any learner (slope ~1 vs 0.69-0.91) and ties the best learner's harvest where clustered (both plateau at ~0.80 of an oracle ceiling), while the learner collects more where resource is scarce (0.33 vs 0.22) and holds tighter per-capita intake. Learning thus buys precision and transfer, not a better allocation; neither message passing nor a centralized critic exceeds it at this budget. We read this not as beating RL, but as evidence that a minimal swarm's physics reaches the equilibrium RL seeks without a learner, a reward, or a trained parameter. A companion paper develops the mechanism. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: SWIFT: Self-guided Weak-to-strong dIFfusion models via Target extrapolation
docs.text:
SWIFT: Self-guided Weak-to-strong dIFfusion models via Target extrapolation SWIFT: Self-guided Weak-to-strong dIFfusion models via Target extrapolation arXiv:2610.25844v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Training high-quality diffusion models is computationally expensive, and inference-time guidance often adds further sampling cost. In this work, we introduce Swift, a simple yet effective self-guided training method that uses a frozen weak denoiser to improve a stronger model without adding inference overhead. For each noisy input, Swift extrapolates the clean regression target away from the weak denoiser's prediction, amplifying components that remain underfit. The weak guide can be an early training checkpoint, requires no backpropagation during main-model training, and is discarded afterward. The resulting model retains the original sampler and supports both conditional and unconditional generation without label dropout or an unconditional branch. We explain this mechanism through a spectral analysis of finite-time population gradient flow in an RKHS. With an early-stopped weak guide, we prove that a nonempty range of extrapolation strengths yields strictly lower posterior-mean error than matched standard training, despite shifting the regression target away from the posterior mean. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256 demonstrate improvements across model scales and representations. In one ImageNet-256 configuration, Swift surpasses the baseline's best FID using roughly half the total training compute, including guide preparation and training overhead. On RAEv2, it achieves FID 1.15 without inference-time guidance and 0.99 with guidance. These results establish target extrapolation as an effective approach to weak-to-strong diffusion training with efficient single-model inference. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Hilbert-Scale Stability of Posterior Diffusion Priors for Ill-Posed Signal Recovery
docs.text:
Hilbert-Scale Stability of Posterior Diffusion Priors for Ill-Posed Signal Recovery Hilbert-Scale Stability of Posterior Diffusion Priors for Ill-Posed Signal Recovery arXiv:2610.27030v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Indirect and noisy observations are difficult to invert when the forward operator smooths out the unknown signal. In this case, the unstable modes are precisely the modes that the data reveals least, thus the success of any reconstruction method depends on how prior information interacts with the geometry of the operator across regularity scales. Diffusion priors have become ubiquitous for such problems; however, the current theory still does not determine when a learned score remains informative under ill-posed forward operators. In this paper, we study posterior diffusion for linear inverse problems on Hilbert scales and derive a stability theory under an explicit score-amplification condition. Under a smoothing condition on the forward map, a source condition on the truth, and weak-norm control of score error, we derive non-asymptotic recovery bounds in \(\Hs^s\) that separate observation noise, score approximation, and reverse-time discretization. These bounds give a recoverable regularity threshold determined jointly by operator smoothing, truth regularity, score regularity, and the posterior correction. The threshold specifies the Hilbert-scale norms \(\Hs^s\) in which weak-norm score error remains controlled after propagation through the posterior reverse dynamics. For larger regularity indices \(s\), the inverse geometry magnifies the same error, and the Hilbert-scale recovery estimate no longer gives uniform stability. We also prove that a posterior correction adapted to the forward operator improves stability relative to isotropic guidance in the regularity ranges where the smoothing action of the forward map matters most. The recovery estimates give a regularity-sensitive theory of posterior diffusion and show how learned score error, operator smoothing, and reconstruction norm jointly determine the stable range predicted by the analysis. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Deep catastrophic-risk-aware reinforcement learning
docs.text:
Deep catastrophic-risk-aware reinforcement learning Deep catastrophic-risk-aware reinforcement learning arXiv:2610.27214v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Estimating extreme risk in reinforcement learning becomes increasingly difficult as the confidence level increases, since only a small number of observations contribute to empirical estimates of Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR). In this paper, we extend an Extreme Value Theory (EVT) approach for CVaR optimization to high-dimensional neural-network policies. Using a peaks-over-threshold representation and method-of-moments estimation, we obtain a differentiable tail-risk objective and show that, conditional on the selected threshold, its finite-sample gradient can be computed directly through automatic differentiation. We first validate the approach in a controlled experiment with a known optimal solution and then investigate its performance in a deep-hedging problem with rare extreme market movements. Our results show similar hedging behavior for EVT- and empirical-CVaR-trained policies under normal conditions, while EVT-trained policies exhibit lower hedging losses under the extreme-scenario evaluation across the training sample sizes considered. These results suggest that EVT can provide a practical alternative for training neural policies when the observations relevant to extreme risk are scarce. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Near-Duplicate Image Selection Transfers Preferences in Vision-Language Models
docs.text:
Near-Duplicate Image Selection Transfers Preferences in Vision-Language Models Near-Duplicate Image Selection Transfers Preferences in Vision-Language Models arXiv:2610.27943v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Subliminal learning is the phenomenon in which a model transmits its preferences to another model through data that do not explicitly express them. As models increasingly curate training data for other models, we ask whether this transfer can arise from choosing among near-duplicate images while keeping the source photographs and human-written captions fixed. We show that this restricted form of image selection is sufficient. For each photograph, a curator selects one of eight near-duplicate variants by caption likelihood, without target-specific prompts. Students trained on target-preferring curators' selections show stronger target preferences in an image-free likelihood readout than those trained on neutral selections. We observe owl preference transfer in LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL, and Gemma 4, with curators and students initialized from the same base checkpoint. The owl transfer results repeat across independently trained curator ensembles and student seeds on a shared image bank, exceed count-matched random reselections, and replicate on a new source bank with new curators in Qwen3-VL. Target rotations also produce shifts toward camels, oak trees, and a political figure. Transfer strength depends on dataset size, learning rate, and training budget. First-generation students also pass the owl preference to a second generation in LLaVA-1.5 and Qwen3-VL through captions that do not explicitly mention owls. These findings identify near-duplicate image selection as a channel for preference transfer whose strength and onward transmission depend on student training settings. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: When Momentum Helps Polyak--Ruppert Averaging
docs.text:
When Momentum Helps Polyak--Ruppert Averaging When Momentum Helps Polyak--Ruppert Averaging arXiv:2610.27990v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Polyak--Ruppert averaging gives SGD and momentum methods the same asymptotic covariance. We characterize how fast finite runs reach it and how far they can be parallelized. For strongly convex quadratics with additive noise, we prove an online--offline bridge: the empirical risk minimizer on the samples of a tail average is one Newton step from the tail-averaged query point of any online procedure. For SGD, heavy ball, and Nesterov's method with constant momentum, this step is a boundary term at the two ends of the tail and splits the gap to the offline estimator into center, covariance, and shape errors. Necessary and sufficient conditions show that, on the least curved direction, the center error sets the pace: SGD needs $m\gg\kappa^2$ rounds but momentum only $m\gg\kappa$, where $\kappa$ is the condition number, so at sample size $N$ the critical batch size grows from $\Theta(\sqrt{N}/\kappa)$ to $\Theta(\sqrt{N/\kappa})$. The covariance error separates the momentum methods: heavy ball has relative variance excess $\Theta(\kappa^{3/2}/m)$ along the stiffest direction, whereas Nesterov has relative error $O(\sqrt{\kappa}/m)$ in every direction. The shape error is method-independent by a Berry--Esseen bound uniform in $\kappa$ and batch size, so confidence intervals are valid when the other two errors vanish. We further examine how the conclusions change under heavy-tailed or state-dependent noise and clipping, and establish a first-order comparison with ERM for nonlinear Nesterov averaging under explicit conditions. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Time Series Foundation Models for Electrical Load Forecasting
docs.text:
Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Time Series Foundation Models for Electrical Load Forecasting Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Time Series Foundation Models for Electrical Load Forecasting arXiv:2610.28200v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Accurate electrical load forecasting supports power-system operation across countries, regions, cities, and buildings, but repeated development of target-specific models is costly. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) provide reusable pretrained backbones, although multi-domain pretraining may not fully capture load-specific characteristics. This paper compares pretrained inference, full fine-tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) in terms of forecasting accuracy and adaptation efficiency across four electrical load aggregation levels. MOIRAI 1.0 Large serves as the primary backbone, while Chronos-2 assesses whether the findings transfer across model families. The evaluation covers both in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) settings and examines whether compact adaptation provides consistent gains over strong pretrained checkpoints. Pretrained foundation models outperform the implemented seasonal naive and XGBoost baselines across the evaluated aggregation levels. On MOIRAI Large, rank-16 LoRA reduces normalized mean absolute error (NMAE) by 7.5% on average while updating 3.146 million parameters, about 1% of the model, and retains most of the improvement from full fine-tuning. Chronos-2 achieves lower pretrained NMAE than MOIRAI, while its relative adaptation gains remain smaller overall. OOD results show that adaptation benefits vary by target, with the clearest gains for the local-area series and several buildings. Overall, LoRA provides a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off when adaptation yields a meaningful gain over a strong pretrained checkpoint. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Scalable Stress-Constrained Topology Optimization: A Simultaneous Approach Based on Machine Learning
docs.text:
Scalable Stress-Constrained Topology Optimization: A Simultaneous Approach Based on Machine Learning Scalable Stress-Constrained Topology Optimization: A Simultaneous Approach Based on Machine Learning arXiv:2610.28703v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large-scale topology optimization (TO) remains computationally demanding, especially for stress-constrained problems. To address this challenge, we propose the simultaneous neural topology optimization (SNTO) framework where state, adjoint, and design variables are represented with custom neural networks (NNs) whose parameters are jointly optimized within a single loop using adjoint analysis and automatic differentiation. The loss function combines the design objective, an aggregation of the local stress constraints, and the potential energy functionals. Our NNs have a unique architecture that accelerates convergence while capturing the sharp gradients and boundaries which are critical to stress-constrained TO. To scale to millions of degrees of freedom, we develop a hardware-aware training scheme in which the design domain is partitioned into subdomains distributed across multiple graphics processing units (GPUs).
